876.title: Nalanda
876.hook: the great monastic university of northern India, with thousands of students
876.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist traditions describe their own monastic study, with memorization and formal debate, as carrying on the Nalanda tradition, and remember the Nalanda masters in their lineages.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahayana, new sutras and a vow for all beings. Your line: for all beings. Today, a place where those sutras, and the older teachings too, were argued over and learned.

At the gate, a monk stops a young traveler and asks him a question. Not his name. A hard question about the teaching. In the account of the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, the keepers of this gate tested newcomers that way, and those who couldn't answer went home. Whoever gets through steps into a world of monasteries, courtyards and lecture halls, crowded with students from near and far, and loud with debate. This is Nalanda, in the old land of Magadha in northern India. Xuanzang studied here himself.
screen: `A QUESTION AT THE GATE.` → `COURTYARDS, LECTURE HALLS, DEBATE.` → `NALANDA.`

segments.voice: First, a place of learning. Nalanda was a monastery, but it worked like a university. Kings and patrons supported it, and monks lived, studied and taught there. In the pilgrims' accounts, the days were full of lectures and debate. Second, more than one subject. Students learned the sutras, Mahayana and older teachings alike, and also logic, grammar and medicine, the tools for reading and arguing well. Debate wasn't a sideline. It was how an idea was tested, the way Nagasena and the king tested theirs. Third, the teachers. Tradition links Nalanda with famous names. Xuanzang's own teacher there was the abbot Shilabhadra. Tibetan tradition says the poet-monk Shantideva lived at Nalanda and recited his Way of the Bodhisattva there, to monks who had thought him lazy. Some traditions connect the philosopher Nagarjuna with the place as well, though the sources don't agree. Fourth, the library. Tibetan accounts give it a name, Dharmaganja, the treasury of the dharma, and name the buildings that held its books: Ratnasagara, ocean of jewels, and others. Whatever its exact size, here texts were copied, kept, argued over and carried away by students who went home to other lands. Much of what later traveled to Tibet and China passed through places like this. A library is a strange kind of treasure. It keeps nothing for itself. It only works when someone opens it, learns, and carries the learning somewhere else.

877.title: The late Indian masters
877.hook: Vikramashila and the teachers who later carried Buddhism to Tibet
877.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism a teaching is usually received through a lineage, and students often learn the names of the teachers who handed it down; Atisha's three kinds of people still frame Tibetan teachings on the stages of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nalanda, the monastery that worked like a university. Your line: the great library.

A request arrives at a monastery in eastern India. It comes from the north, from Tibet, and it asks for one teacher by name. The Tibetan histories tell it as a long courtship: messengers, gifts of gold, a refusal, then a second try. The teacher they wanted was a senior monk at the monastery of Vikramashila, known in Tibet as Atisha. His own monastery did not want to give him up, and tradition says it let him go only for a time, expecting him back. In the end he went, crossed the mountains, and taught in Tibet until he died there.
screen: `A REQUEST FROM TIBET.` → `ONE TEACHER, BY NAME.` → `ATISHA OF VIKRAMASHILA.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Vikramashila stood in eastern India, a monastery that tradition says was founded and supported by kings. Like Nalanda, it was a place of study: monks trained in philosophy, debate, meditation and ritual, and its leading teachers were honored by name. Second, the man. Atisha's monastic name was Dipankara Shrijnana. Tradition says he studied with many teachers, in India and, by some accounts, across the sea in a land called Suvarnadvipa, the golden island. Third, the book. In Tibet, Atisha wrote a short work called the Lamp for the Path to Awakening. It sorts practitioners into three kinds of people: those who seek a better life to come, those who seek their own freedom, and those who seek awakening for the sake of all beings. Each stage, it says, rests on the one before, the way a second floor rests on a first. Tibetan teachers later built long teachings on the stages of the path on that frame, and his close Tibetan student, Dromtonpa, gathered his followers into the Kadampa tradition. Fourth, the thread. Atisha was not alone. In these generations Indian teachers traveled north and Tibetan translators traveled south to study, and the learning of the Indian monasteries crossed the mountains in their heads and in their luggage. Tibetan lineages still keep the names, teacher to student, back to the halls of India. Behind a teaching given in Tibet today stands a chain of people, and some of the links were monks at Vikramashila.

878.title: The fading in India
878.hook: Buddhism slowly waned in India; historians give many reasons and still debate them
878.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often read the passages about the decline of the true teaching as a call to keep their own practice sincere, and historians of India continue to study and debate why Buddhism faded there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Atisha, crossing the mountains to Tibet. Your line: the last Indian masters.

"All created things perish." That is the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, and the texts don't exempt the teaching itself. In one sutta the Buddha speaks plainly about a time when the true teaching could disappear. In India, where he walked and taught, the monasteries did grow quiet. Not in a day: slowly, over generations, region by region, the robes and the chanting thinned out in many places where they had once been common. Ask why, and you won't get one answer.
screen: `ALL CREATED THINGS PERISH.` → `THE MONASTERIES GROW QUIET.` → `WHY? NOT ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the monasteries. In its later centuries in India, much of Buddhist life gathered in large monasteries supported by kings and wealthy donors. Some historians suggest that when that support shifted, the monasteries had fewer roots in village life to fall back on. Second, the neighbors. Hindu devotional movements grew strong in the same regions, and some Buddhist images, ideas and holy places were drawn into the wider religious life around them. Some Hindu texts came to count the Buddha himself among the forms of Vishnu. Historians describe a slow blending, not a single moment. Third, violence. Raids sacked great monasteries and scattered their monks. That is tomorrow's story. Fourth, the debate itself. Historians weigh these reasons differently, and they are still arguing. Some stress the raids; others stress the long, quiet changes before them. Some point out that the story differs region by region, and that the practice never vanished entirely. So the honest summary is today's line: many reasons. The sutta offers a view from inside the tradition. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha says the true teaching is not made to disappear by earth, water, fire or wind. It fades when a counterfeit of the teaching appears, the way real gold disappears from the world once counterfeit gold appears, and when people lose respect for the teacher, the teaching, the community, the training and concentration. Some Buddhist teachers read that passage as a warning to look first at themselves, not at outside causes.

On each out-breath, let it be what it is: something that mattered, and changed.

879.title: Nalanda burned
879.hook: around 1200 the great monasteries were sacked and burned; the libraries were lost
879.howItsDone: Buddhists remember the destruction of the great Indian monasteries in teaching and pilgrimage, and the ruins of Nalanda are visited today by pilgrims and students from across the Buddhist world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: saddhamma, and why it faded in India. Your line: many reasons.

A Tibetan pilgrim walks into the ruins of Nalanda. His name is Dharmasvamin, and the account of his travels, written down by a student, describes what he found: halls damaged and deserted, most of the monks gone. And in the middle of the ruins, an old teacher named Rahula Shribhadra, still teaching his students. Raiders had already come through. The account says they would come again while the pilgrim was there.
screen: `A PILGRIM IN THE RUINS.` → `AN OLD TEACHER, STILL TEACHING.` → `NALANDA BURNED.`

segments.voice: First, the raids. As armies conquered northern India, they attacked the great monasteries of the east. A Persian chronicle of the period describes soldiers storming what they took for a fortress, finding it full of books and shaven-headed men, and only afterward learning it had been a place of study. Historians debate which monastery that passage describes, and whether Nalanda fell in one attack or was damaged over years. Second, the libraries. These monasteries kept manuscripts copied by hand on palm leaf and bark, and later accounts say the libraries burned. Some texts survived because monks carried them away, or because copies had already traveled to Tibet, Nepal or China. Some Buddhist works now survive only in translation, with no Sanskrit original known. Third, the people. Monks were killed or scattered, and some fled north into the mountains, carrying what they could. Fourth, the witness. The pilgrim's account shows the place was not simply erased. A teacher still taught. A student still came. When the soldiers returned, the account says, the old teacher would not leave, so the pilgrim carried him on his back to a hiding place, and they waited until the danger passed. Then they went on with the lessons. The tradition teaches impermanence. Here it is in smoke and ash: generations of learning gone, and an old teacher and his student, back at the books.

880.title: Where it held on
880.hook: in Nepal's Newar communities, the Himalayas and the hills of Bengal, the practice continued
880.howItsDone: Newar Buddhists in the Kathmandu Valley gather in courtyard monasteries for rituals led by Vajracharya priests, and Buddhist communities in the Himalayas and the hills of Bangladesh and eastern India keep their own temples and festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nalanda burned, and what made it through the fire. Your line: the libraries burned.

In the Kathmandu Valley, in the courtyard of an old monastery, a man in ordinary clothes opens a manuscript in Sanskrit and begins a ritual. He is a Vajracharya, a priest of Newar Buddhism. He may be married, with children, and tradition says the role passes down through families. No lifelong robes, no monastery to sleep in, just a household and a family calling. And yet the texts he honors come from the same world as the great monasteries of India.
screen: `A COURTYARD IN KATHMANDU.` → `A PRIEST WITH A FAMILY.` → `TEXTS FROM THE OLD MONASTERIES.`

segments.voice: First, Nepal. The Newar people of the Kathmandu Valley kept a form of Buddhism that grew from the same Sanskrit tradition as the Indian monasteries. Its priests, the Vajracharyas, and householder families called Shakyas live around courtyards that still carry the old name vihara, monastery. Newar Buddhists keep Sanskrit texts, like the Perfection of Wisdom, and honor them in worship. When scholars went looking for Sanskrit Buddhist works lost in India, some of the manuscripts turned up in Nepal. Second, the Himalayas. Higher in the mountains, in places like Ladakh and Sikkim and the high valleys of Nepal, the practice continued in the forms that had traveled to Tibet: monasteries on ridges, prayer flags, chanting in Tibetan. Third, the hills of Bengal. In the far east of the old Bengal region, communities such as the Barua and the Chakma kept Buddhist practice alive in their villages, with monks and festivals of their own. Fourth, what that changes. The story of Buddhism in India is often told with an ending. These communities complicate it. Small, often far from the cities, sometimes under pressure, they kept going: a family priesthood, a mountain monastery, a village temple with a few monks. Nothing dramatic. Just the same rituals, done again next week, and the week after.

881.title: The great chronicle
881.hook: the Mahavamsa, Sri Lanka's chronicle of kings and monks (Geiger, 1912)
881.carry: made for the serene joy of the faithful
881.howItsDone: In Sri Lanka the Mahavamsa is read in schools and monasteries and retold at temples and festivals as the story of how the teaching came to the island, while historians study it alongside inscriptions and archaeology.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Vajracharya, and where the practice held on. Your line: it held on.

The author opens by finding fault. An older telling of this history exists, he says in his first lines, but it is too long in some places, too short in others, and full of repetition. So he will tell it again, in verse, free of those faults. That's how the Mahavamsa begins, Sri Lanka's chronicle of kings and monks, here in Wilhelm Geiger's English translation. Tradition names its author as a monk called Mahanama.
screen: `A HISTORY, TOLD AGAIN.` → `TOO LONG HERE, TOO SHORT THERE.` → `THE MAHAVAMSA.`

segments.voice: First, how it begins. Before a single king, the chronicle brings the Buddha to the island. Its first chapter tells of three visits: one to drive out the yakkhas, spirits who held the land; one to settle a quarrel between two serpent kings fighting over a jeweled throne; and one to Kelaniya, at a serpent king's invitation. Before the history starts, the chronicle lays a blessing on the land. Second, what it covers: kings and monks, side by side. Who built which stupa, who brought which relic, who supported the monasteries and who neglected them. It judges kings partly by how they treated the teaching. Third, what it says it is for. Its chapters close by naming their purpose: the work was made for the serene joy and the stirring of the faithful. The book tells you plainly it isn't neutral. It is history written to move its readers. Fourth, how it is read now. Historians use it with care, checking it against inscriptions and ruins; they find it valuable and also shaped by its aims. Buddhists in Sri Lanka read it as the story of how the teaching came to their island and was kept there. Some of its war stories are read in very different ways by different readers today. A chronicle like this is a community telling its own story, with love and with a point of view. Knowing both is part of reading it well.
screen: `THE BUDDHA VISITS THE ISLAND.` · `KINGS AND MONKS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `WRITTEN FOR THE JOY OF THE FAITHFUL.` · `READ WITH LOVE AND WITH CARE.` · then, large: `A COMMUNITY TELLS ITS STORY.`

882.title: Buddhaghosa arrives
882.hook: the scholar comes to Sri Lanka and writes the great commentaries in Pali
882.howItsDone: Theravada monks study the Visuddhimagga and the Pali commentaries alongside the suttas, and teachers draw on them to explain the meaning of words and passages in the canon.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mahavamsa, Sri Lanka's chronicle of kings and monks. Your line: made for the serene joy of the faithful.
screen: `MADE FOR THE SERENE JOY OF THE FAITHFUL.`

segments.voice: Tangled within, tangled without, and people everywhere caught in the knots. Who can work them loose? In a short sutta, a question like that is put to the Buddha, and he answers in a single verse. Much later, a scholar from India built an entire book on that one verse. The chronicle remembers him as Buddhaghosa, and says he crossed to Sri Lanka to study the old commentaries kept at the Great Monastery in Anuradhapura.
screen: `TANGLED WITHIN, TANGLED WITHOUT.` → `ONE VERSE IN ANSWER.` → `A SCHOLAR CROSSES THE SEA.`

segments.voice: First, why he came. The later part of the chronicle says Buddhaghosa was a learned man in India who heard that the commentaries on the Buddha's discourses were kept in Sri Lanka, in the Sinhala language. So he went to study them at the Great Monastery, the Mahavihara. Second, the test. The elders, the story says, didn't simply hand over their library. They gave him verses and asked him to show what he could do. At the heart of his answer is the Buddha's reply to the tangle: a wise person, established in virtue, developing mind and understanding, can untangle the tangle. His answer became the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification: a long, careful map of virtue, concentration and wisdom, all hung on that one verse. Third, the legend. The story says the gods hid his finished book, and he wrote it again; they hid it once more, and he wrote it a third time. Read side by side, the copies agreed word for word. Some readers take that as a miracle. Others read it as the tradition's way of saying this work can be trusted. Fourth, the commentaries. Tradition credits him with rendering the Sinhala commentaries into Pali, the language of the texts, so monks anywhere could read them. Theravada teachers still turn to those commentaries to explain what a word in a sutta means. When a monk somewhere explains a difficult line, Buddhaghosa may well be in the room.
screen: `HE COMES FOR THE COMMENTARIES.` · `THE ELDERS TEST HIM.` · `THREE COPIES, WORD FOR WORD.` · `THE COMMENTARIES, IN PALI.` · then, large: `UNTANGLE THE TANGLE.`

segments.voice: Take today's verse in plain words: established in virtue, developing mind and understanding, one can untangle the tangle. Hold one piece at a time for a few breaths, steady footing, the mind as it is right now, one tangle you'd like to see clearly, without hurrying to answers.
Buddhaghosa arrives. The scholar from India who came to Sri Lanka, wrote the Path of Purification, and is credited with putting the old commentaries into Pali. Today's word.

chat.says: Why do Theravada monks still read Buddhaghosa?
options: His Path of Purification and Pali explanations still help monks understand the Buddha's talks.
He was the Buddha's own helper, and he wrote down every one of the Buddha's talks.
He translated the Buddha's talks from Pali into the Sinhala language.
chat.meaning: Tradition credits him with putting the Sinhala commentaries into Pali, and his Visuddhimagga maps virtue, concentration and wisdom. Teachers still use both.
